notes: One who rescues or saves. In Luke it is first used by Mary of God (1:47) and then by the angel of Jesus (2:11). In the Roman world "savior" was a title given to emperors and benefactors, so using it for a baby in a feeding trough is a pointed contrast.

range.note: A royal or divine title in the Greek world.

elsewhere.note: "Indeed the Savior of the world."
God exalted him to be Leader and Savior.
From David's seed, God brought a Savior.
We eagerly await a Savior.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: The verb behind "gospel." Luke uses it more than any other Gospel: Gabriel announces John's birth (1:19), the angel announces Jesus' birth (2:10), John preaches (3:18), and Jesus says it is why he was sent (4:18, 4:43). It means to bring news worth celebrating, as a messenger from a battlefield would.

elsewhere.note: The poor have good news preached to them.
Philip tells him the good news about Jesus.
How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news.
The good news was preached to us.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: Favor, kindness freely given, and the gratitude that answers it. Mary has "found favor" with God (1:30), the child Jesus grows in favor with God and people (2:40, 2:52), and the Nazarenes marvel at his "gracious" words (4:22).

elsewhere.note: The Word was full of grace and truth.
Great grace was on them all.
Justified freely by his grace.
By grace you are saved.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: Release or letting go, used for freeing a prisoner, canceling a debt, and forgiving sins. In Luke 4:18 Jesus reads Isaiah's "release to the captives" and "set free those who are oppressed," using the same word twice. Forgiveness of sins is tied to John's baptism (3:3) and Zechariah's song (1:77).

elsewhere.note: The blood poured out for the forgiveness of sins.
Be baptized for the forgiveness of sins.
Redemption, the forgiveness of sins.
Without shedding of blood, no forgiveness.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: A change of mind that leads to a change of life. John's baptism is "of repentance" (3:3), and he asks for "fruits worthy of repentance" (3:8), and then spells it out as sharing, honesty, and fairness. It is the noun that goes with the verb "repent" (metanoeō).

elsewhere.note: Produce fruit worthy of repentance.
Repentance toward God.
God's kindness leads you to repentance.
Godly sorrow produces repentance.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: Fruit of a tree or a field, and so the result of a life. John says that repentance must show in "fruits" and warns that a tree that doesn't produce good fruit is cut down (3:8-9). Elizabeth also uses it, literally, of Mary's child (1:42).

elsewhere.note: You will know them by their fruits.
Whoever remains in me bears much fruit.
The fruit of the Spirit.
Wisdom from above is full of good fruits.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: From a verb meaning "to throw across," so one who accuses or slanders. In the New Testament it is the name for the chief adversary, also called Satan. In Luke 4 he tests Jesus three times and leaves "until another time."

elsewhere.note: Jesus was led up to be tempted by the devil.
"You are of your father the devil."
Stand against the schemes of the devil.
Resist the devil, and he will flee.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: To dip or immerse. John's baptism in the Jordan was a sign of repentance (3:3), and Luke has Jesus baptized while he prays (3:21). John says the one to come will baptize "with the Holy Spirit and fire" (3:16).

elsewhere.note: Jesus comes to John to be baptized.
Jesus is baptized in the Jordan.
Be baptized for the forgiveness of sins.
Baptized into his death.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: Authority, the right and the power to act. In Luke 4 people are astonished that Jesus' word carries authority, in teaching (4:32) and over unclean spirits (4:36).

range.note: Permission or freedom to do something.
The ability to make things happen.
Authority over others, or the people who hold it.

elsewhere.note: All authority has been given to me.
The right to become children of God.
Governing authorities.
Delivered from the power of darkness.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: To rebuke, to speak sharply to. In Luke 4 Jesus rebukes the unclean spirit (4:35), the fever (4:39), and the demons, and does not let them speak (4:41), as a master commands what is under him.

range.note: Give a strict order, often to silence.

elsewhere.note: He rebukes the wind and the sea.
Jesus rebukes the unclean spirit.
"The Lord rebuke you."

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: A word that can mean "sir," "master," or "Lord," and which the Greek Old Testament uses for God's name. Luke uses it of God throughout the birth story and then increasingly of Jesus, who is called "the Lord" in his narration (7:13). Peter's "Lord" in 5:8 begins with awe; in 6:46 Jesus asks why people say it without doing what he says.

range.note: The title for God and for Jesus.

elsewhere.note: "Not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord.'"
Thomas: "My Lord and my God!"
God has made him both Lord and Christ.
Every tongue will confess that Jesus Christ is Lord.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: Someone who collected taxes or customs for Rome, usually by paying for the contract in advance and recovering the cost, plus a profit, from the public. They were thought of as collaborators and thieves and are grouped with "sinners." Luke names tax collectors more than any other Gospel: Levi (5:27), those baptized by John (3:12, 7:29), and later Zacchaeus (19:2).

range.note: One who collects tolls on trade.

elsewhere.note: Many tax collectors and sinners sat with him.
Tax collectors and prostitutes go into the kingdom ahead of you.
Tax collectors came to be baptized.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: From the same root as charis (grace). It means to give as a favor, and is used for forgiving a debt. In the story of the two debtors, the moneylender "forgave" both (7:42-43). Paul uses it too (2 Corinthians 2:7; Colossians 3:13).

elsewhere.note: You should rather forgive and comfort him.
Forgiving each other, as God forgave you.
Forgive as the Lord forgave you.
Will he not also freely give us all things?

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: A sinner. In Luke it is used of people the religious leaders consider outside the community: tax collectors (5:30, 7:34), the woman in Simon's house (7:37, 7:39), and Peter himself, who says, "I am a sinful man" (5:8). Jesus says he came to call sinners to repentance (5:32).

range.note: Someone seen as outside the faithful community.

elsewhere.note: Not the righteous, but sinners.
God doesn't listen to sinners.
While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
Christ came into the world to save sinners.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: Blessed, fortunate, or happy in the sense of being in a favored position before God. In Luke's version the blessing is given to those who are actually poor, hungry, and weeping (6:20-22), and is paired with warnings to the rich.

range.note: In God's favor, whatever things look like now.
In ordinary Greek, simply happy or prosperous.

elsewhere.note: Blessed are the poor in spirit.
Blessed are those who have not seen and yet believe.
Blessed is the one who endures trial.
Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: "Woe," a cry of grief or warning. Luke gives four woes to match his four blessings (6:24-26). Throughout the Gospel it is spoken of those whose comfort has become their security.

range.note: A prophet's announcement of trouble ahead.

elsewhere.note: Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees.
Woe is me if I do not preach the gospel.
Woe to them, for they walked in the way of Cain.
Woe to those who dwell on the earth.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: The verb of self-giving love. In Luke 6 Jesus says to love enemies, which is unlike ordinary loyalty, since even sinners love those who love them (6:32). In 7:42-47 love is the response of a forgiven person.

range.note: Care for another that shows itself in action.

elsewhere.note: Love your enemies.
Love one another as I have loved you.
Love is the fulfillment of the law.
We love because he first loved us.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: Someone sent with authority. Luke says Jesus chose twelve from his disciples "whom he also named apostles" (6:13), after a night of prayer.

range.note: Someone sent to act with the sender's authority.
The twelve, and later others such as Paul.

elsewhere.note: A messenger is not greater than the one who sent him.
Matthias is numbered with the eleven apostles.
Paul, called to be an apostle.
An apostle not from men.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: The Sabbath, the seventh day of rest. Luke 6 gives two Sabbath conflicts, over picking grain and healing a hand, ending with "The Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath."

range.note: The seventh day, set apart for rest.
As in "the first day of the week" (28:1).

elsewhere.note: The Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.
It was the Sabbath on that day.
They went into the synagogue on the Sabbath.
Don't let anyone judge you about a Sabbath.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: To be moved in the gut. In Luke it is used of Jesus' reaction to the widow of Nain (7:13), and in two stories only Luke tells it is used of the good Samaritan (10:33) and the father in the story of the lost son (15:20).

range.note: The feeling that leads to help.

elsewhere.note: Compassion before feeding the crowd.
Moved with pity for a man with a skin disease.
Moved with compassion for two blind men.
Compassion for the crowd like sheep without a shepherd.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: Trust, faithfulness, and belief. In Luke it is what Jesus finds in the centurion (7:9) and the forgiven woman (7:50), and what he asks of the disciples in the storm (8:25).

range.note: Confidence in a person or what they can do.
Being trustworthy and loyal (STEPBible tags this sense separately).

elsewhere.note: Your faith has made you well.
The righteous will live by faith.
By grace you have been saved through faith.
Faith is the assurance of things hoped for.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

gloss: to save, to heal, to make well
notes: To save, heal, or make well, one word covering rescue, healing, and salvation. In Luke 7:50 and 8:48 Jesus says to women, "Your faith has saved you" or "made you well," which can mean either, or both.

range.note: To save from danger or death.
To save in the fullest sense.

elsewhere.note: He will save his people from their sins.
The world might be saved through him.
Everyone who calls will be saved.
By grace you are saved.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: A Latin loan word for a unit of several thousand Roman soldiers. The spirits give it as their name (8:30), since they are many.

elsewhere.note: More than twelve legions of angels.
The same name in Mark's telling.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: A comparison or story set beside a truth. In Luke 8 Jesus tells the parable of the sower and says that for the crowds the truths are given in parables, while the disciples are given the meaning.

range.note: One thing set beside another to explain it.
A short story with a point, like the sower.
A saying that needs thinking about.

elsewhere.note: He spoke in parables.
He taught them many things in parables.
A symbol for the present time.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: To wait on someone, as at a table. In Luke 8:3 the women "provided for" Jesus and the twelve from their possessions, using the same verb as for serving at table.

range.note: Serve in a role of care or leadership.

elsewhere.note: The Son of Man came to serve.
She served them.
Whoever serves me must follow me.
Serving tables.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: Literally "the way out." Moses and Elijah speak with Jesus about "his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem" (9:31). It is the same word as the book of Exodus, so Luke gives Jesus' death and resurrection the shape of a new rescue. In 2 Peter 1:15 the same word is used for Peter's own death.

range.note: A way out, or an exit.

elsewhere.note: Joseph spoke of the departure (exodos) of the sons of Israel.
After my departure.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: Splendor, honor, and the visible presence of God. The angels' "glory" at the birth (2:9, 2:14) becomes the glory of Jesus on the mountain (9:31-32) and again in the future coming (21:27). The root is "to seem," so it can mean reputation, but in the Bible it is the weight and brightness of God.

elsewhere.note: We have seen his glory.
All have fallen short of the glory of God.
The light of the knowledge of the glory of God.
He is the radiance of God's glory.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: Literally "the one near." It is the word in the command to love your neighbor as yourself (Leviticus 19:18, in the Greek Bible). The lawyer asks "Who is my neighbor?" and Jesus' story reverses it: the Samaritan became a neighbor by what he did (10:36).

elsewhere.note: You shall love your neighbor as yourself.
Love does no harm to a neighbor.
The whole law is fulfilled in one word.
Love your neighbor as yourself.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: Peace in the full Hebrew sense of shalom: well-being, wholeness, and right relationship, not just the absence of war. The seventy are to say "Peace to this house" (10:5-6). Luke's Gospel is full of the word: the angels' "on earth peace" (2:14), "Go in peace" (7:50, 8:48), and the risen Jesus' greeting (24:36).

elsewhere.note: Let your peace come on the house.
My peace I give to you.
We have peace with God.
The peace of God that surpasses understanding.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: The noun for service, especially waiting on someone at a table. Martha is "distracted with much serving" (10:40). The word is later used for the work of the church, and gives us "deacon."

elsewhere.note: The daily distribution.
Whoever has a gift of service.
Varieties of service.
The ministry of reconciliation.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: To treat as holy or to set apart for God. "Hallowed be your name" (11:2) asks that God's name be honored as holy, as in the Old Testament, where God says he will make his name holy among the nations (Ezekiel 36:23).

elsewhere.note: Hallowed be your name.
For their sakes I sanctify myself.
He who sanctifies and those who are sanctified.
In your hearts, honor Christ as Lord.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: A word found in the Lord's Prayer and nowhere else in Greek writing that survives. It is usually translated "daily," but it may mean "for the coming day" or "needed for existence." Luke adds "day by day" (11:3), which supports a sense of daily provision.

elsewhere.note: Give us this day our daily bread.

uncertain: The exact meaning of epiousios is debated because the word doesn't survive anywhere else in ancient Greek.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: A test or trial, which can be meant to prove someone or to lead them to fail. "Bring us not into temptation" (11:4) asks not to be put to a test that is too much. The same word is used for Jesus' testing in the wilderness (4:13) and the disciples' trial in Gethsemane (22:40, 22:46).

elsewhere.note: Do not lead us into temptation.
No temptation has taken you but such as is common.
Count it all joy when you meet trials.
The Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: Breath, wind, or spirit, in Greek and in the Hebrew word ruach behind it. In Luke it most often refers to the Holy Spirit, who fills John, Mary, Elizabeth, Zechariah, Simeon, and Jesus; it also refers to unclean spirits. Luke and Acts together are often called the Gospel of the Spirit.

range.note: The Holy Spirit, or a spirit being.
Life, the breath of a person.

elsewhere.note: The wind blows where it wishes.
God is spirit.
They were all filled with the Holy Spirit.
Those led by the Spirit of God are sons of God.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: Literally "missing the mark." Luke often pairs it with forgiveness: John's baptism is for the forgiveness of sins (3:3), and the Lord's Prayer asks, "Forgive us our sins" (11:4). It is the noun that goes with hamartolos, "sinner."

range.note: A wrong against God or others.

elsewhere.note: He will save his people from their sins.
The Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world.
The wages of sin is death.
If we confess our sins.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: To be pulled in different directions, to worry. Jesus says not to be anxious about food or clothing (12:22, 12:25-26); Martha is "anxious and troubled about many things" (10:41). The root meaning is to be divided, as in a mind pulled apart.

elsewhere.note: Do not be anxious about your life.
Do not be anxious about anything.
Which of you by worrying can add a cubit to his life?
I want you to be free from anxieties.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: From "to have more." Not just wanting things but wanting more than one's share. Jesus says, "Keep yourselves from covetousness, for a man's life doesn't consist of the abundance of the things which he possesses" (12:15). Paul calls it idolatry (Colossians 3:5).

elsewhere.note: Out of the heart come greed, deceit.
Filled with covetousness.
Let covetousness not be named among you.
Covetousness, which is idolatry.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: The self or life of a person, and the word the rich man addresses (12:19). It covers both "soul" and "life": "Soul, you have many goods laid up" and "tonight your soul is required of you" use the same word as "don't be anxious for your life" (12:22-23).

elsewhere.note: Fear him who can destroy both soul and body.
What does it profit a man to forfeit his soul?
The good shepherd lays down his life.
About three thousand souls were added.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: A stake or cross, the Roman instrument of execution. In Luke Jesus says that following him means to "take up his cross daily" (9:23), adding "daily" to the other Gospels' version.

range.note: The wooden frame used for crucifixion.
A picture of giving up one's life.

elsewhere.note: The same call in Matthew.
The same call in Mark.
The word of the cross.
Boasting only in the cross.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: A kingdom, a rule or reign. In Luke the kingdom is God's reign breaking in: "The Kingdom of God has come near to you" (10:9), and "the Kingdom of God has come to you" (11:20), as his works show.

range.note: The right and power to rule.
The people or territory a king rules.
The age when God's will is done on earth as in heaven.

elsewhere.note: The kingdom of heaven is at hand.
The kingdom of God is at hand.
My kingdom is not of this world.
Speaking of the kingdom of God.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: Named for the valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem. Jesus uses it for final judgment: "Fear him who has power to cast into Gehenna" (12:5).
uncertain: A popular claim says Gehenna was Jerusalem's burning garbage dump. Scholars debate this: the idea isn't found in sources before the Middle Ages, and the Old Testament links the valley with child sacrifice.

range.note: The Valley of Hinnom near Jerusalem.
A picture of final judgment by fire.

elsewhere.note: Whoever says "You fool" is liable to Gehenna.
Better to enter life crippled than with two hands go to Gehenna.
The tongue is set on fire by Gehenna.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: To be awake, keep watch. In Luke 12 the servants whom the master finds "awake" are blessed (12:37, 12:39), and the Son of Man comes when you least expect.

range.note: Stay ready for what is coming.

elsewhere.note: Watch therefore.
Watch and pray.
Let us watch and be sober.
Be sober, be watchful.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: To compete in a contest or fight, from the same root as "agony." Jesus says, "Strive to enter in by the narrow door" (13:24). Paul uses the same word of running a race (1 Corinthians 9:25) and fighting the good fight (1 Timothy 6:12).

elsewhere.note: Every athlete competes with self-control.
I toil, struggling with all his energy.
Fight the good fight of the faith.
My servants would fight.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: Not just poor but reduced to begging, with nothing to fall back on. The word appears more in Luke than any other Gospel: good news to the poor (4:18), "Blessed are you who are poor" (6:20), the guests of the banquet (14:13, 14:21), Lazarus (16:20, 16:22), and the widow's offering (21:3).

elsewhere.note: The poor have good news preached to them.
Give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven.
God chose those who are poor in the world.
Remember the poor.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: To hate, and in the Semitic idiom to love less or to turn away from. Jesus says disciples must "hate" their families and even their own lives (14:26). The parallel in Matthew 10:37 says, "He who loves father or mother more than me isn't worthy of me," which shows the hyperbole.

elsewhere.note: If the world hates you, know that it hated me first.
He who hates his life in this world will keep it.
"Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated."
He will hate the one and love the other.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: To take leave of someone or to give something up. It is used of saying farewell to family (9:61) and of renouncing possessions (14:33). Jesus' point is the same: nothing should have the final claim except him.

elsewhere.note: After he had taken leave of them, he went up the mountain.
Paul took leave of the brothers.
I took leave of them and went on to Macedonia.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

gloss: to lose, to destroy, to perish
notes: To lose or be lost, and also to destroy or perish. In chapter 15 it is the word of the lost sheep, coin, and son. The father says, "he was lost, and is found" (15:24, 15:32). It is the same word Jesus uses when he says he came "to seek and to save that which was lost" (19:10).

elsewhere.note: Go to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.
Whoever believes in him will not perish.
The word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing.
Not wishing that any should perish.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: Joy, gladness, and the celebration that follows. Luke is the Gospel of joy: the angels bring "good news of great joy" (2:10), and the three lost things stories end in joy (15:7, 15:10, 15:32). It's related to charis, "grace."

elsewhere.note: They rejoiced with exceedingly great joy.
That my joy may be in you.
The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace.
For the joy set before him he endured the cross.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: A household manager, the person in charge of a master's property. The word gives us "economy." The dishonest manager of 16:1-8 is one; Paul calls himself a steward of God's mysteries (1 Corinthians 4:1). Jesus also uses it of the faithful servant in 12:42.

range.note: One in charge of the household.

elsewhere.note: Servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God.
An overseer, as God's steward.
Good stewards of God's varied grace.
Erastus, the city treasurer.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

gloss: Hades, the place of the dead
notes: The Greek name for the realm of the dead, used in the Greek Old Testament for Sheol. In the story of the rich man and Lazarus, the rich man is "in Hades, in torment" (16:23), while Lazarus is with Abraham. How literally to take the picture is debated.

range.note: The place where the dead go.
A place of anguish in this story.

elsewhere.note: The gates of Hades will not prevail.
You will not abandon my soul to Hades.
I have the keys of Death and of Hades.
Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire.

uncertain: How literally to read the details of Hades, the gulf, and Abraham's bosom in Luke 16 is debated.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: To change one's mind, to repent. Jesus' call in Luke 13 is to everyone: "Unless you repent, you will all perish" (13:3, 13:5). In Luke 16:30 the rich man thinks a visitor from the dead would make his brothers repent.

range.note: Regret and leave behind what was wrong.
A new direction for the whole life.

elsewhere.note: Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.
Repent, and believe in the gospel.
Repent and be baptized.
Remember from where you have fallen, and repent.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: An Aramaic word for money or property, treated by Jesus as a rival master. "You can't serve God and mammon" (16:13), and Luke applies it to the Pharisees who loved money (16:14).

range.note: Wealth treated as something people serve.

elsewhere.note: You cannot serve God and mammon.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: A word meaning "inside" or "in the midst of." Jesus says the kingdom of God is "entos hymon" (17:21), which can be read "within you" or "among you." Since he is speaking to Pharisees, many take it as "among you," meaning present in his own ministry; others take it as inward. The meaning is debated.

range.note: In the midst of a group.

elsewhere.note: Clean the inside of the cup.

uncertain: Whether Luke 17:21 means "within you" or "among you" is debated.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: To be thankful, and to say so. It comes from charis (grace) and gives us "Eucharist." The Samaritan who returns is the one who "gave him thanks" (17:16); Jesus gives thanks over the bread at the Last Supper (22:19).

elsewhere.note: He gave thanks and broke the loaves.
Jesus gave thanks and distributed the loaves.
They did not give thanks to him.
Give thanks in all circumstances.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: To have pity and to act on it. People call out to Jesus with it throughout Luke: the lepers (17:13), the blind man (18:38-39), and the rich man in Hades (16:24). The related noun is eleos, "mercy."

elsewhere.note: Two blind men cry, "Have mercy on us, Son of David!"
Should you not have had mercy on your fellow servant?
I will have mercy on whom I have mercy.
Have mercy on those who doubt.

notes: A word from the language of the temple, meaning to make atonement or to be reconciled, and by extension to show mercy. The tax collector prays, "God, be merciful to me, a sinner" (18:13), using it. Hebrews 2:17 uses it of Jesus making atonement for the people's sins.

elsewhere.note: To make propitiation for the sins of the people.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: To declare someone in the right. The tax collector goes home "justified" (18:14), declared right with God, not the Pharisee who has made his own case. The word is central to Paul's letters (Romans 3:24, Galatians 2:16). In Luke 7:35 and 7:29 it is used of vindicating or acknowledging God's wisdom.

elsewhere.note: Justified by his grace as a gift.
Since we have been justified by faith.
Not justified by works of the law.
Justified by his grace.

notes: A unit of money, about a hundred days' wages. In the parable, the servants are each given a mina to trade with (19:13, 19:16-25). Matthew's similar parable uses talents, a far larger sum.

range.note: A sum of money worth about a hundred denarii.

notes: From a verb meaning "to look on, to care for." It is the word Jesus uses for "the time of your visitation" (19:44), a time when God came to Jerusalem, and which the city did not recognize. The same root gives "bishop," an overseer (1 Timothy 3:1).

elsewhere.note: Let another take his office.
If anyone aspires to the office of overseer.
On the day of visitation.

notes: "Loved," and often "only and dearly loved." In the parable the owner sends his "beloved son" (20:13), echoing the voice at Jesus' baptism and transfiguration, "This is my beloved Son" (3:22, 9:35).

elsewhere.note: This is my beloved Son.
You are my beloved Son.
To all those in Rome who are loved by God.
Beloved, let us love one another.

notes: A tax paid by a subject people to a ruling power, as distinct from customs duties. The spies ask whether it is lawful to pay tribute to Caesar (20:22). Paul says the same word in Romans 13:6-7.

range.note: A tax paid to a ruler.

elsewhere.note: They accuse him of forbidding giving tribute to Caesar.
For this reason you also pay taxes.
Pay taxes to whom taxes are due.

notes: Literally "standing up again." It is used of the resurrection of the dead. The Sadducees deny it (20:27), and Jesus teaches that those who attain it are "children of the resurrection" (20:36). It also names a theme of Simeon's prophecy, "the falling and rising of many" (2:34).

elsewhere.note: Sadducees say there is no resurrection.
I am the resurrection and the life.
Proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection from the dead.
How can some of you say there is no resurrection?

notes: To let go, to send away, to forgive. In Luke 17:3-4 Jesus says to forgive a brother who repents, up to seven times a day.

range.note: Let someone off what they owe.
Release someone from sin or offense.

elsewhere.note: Forgive us our debts.
Your sins are forgiven.
If you forgive anyone his sins.
If we confess our sins, he forgives us.

A thief and a robber climbs in another way.

Danger from robbers.
